content_blocks.title: Practice reasoning
content_blocks.text: IsolationForest is an unsupervised detector that scores unusual observations relative to the fitted sample. It does not know whether an observation is truly harmful or erroneous. For anomaly detection workflows, keep the problem definition, data selection, estimator configuration, and evaluation criterion explicit. When results are uncertain, compare a baseline and inspect examples rather than treating one metric as a complete explanation.

content_blocks.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
X = [[0.0], [0.1], [-0.1], [0.2], [8.0]]
model = IsolationForest(random_state=0, contamination=0.2).fit(X)
print(model.predict([[8.0]])[0] == -1)

Install the course-compatible dependencies with `python -m pip install scikit-learn numpy scipy pandas matplotlib joblib`. Save the snippet as `main.py` and run `python main.py`. content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and fixed random seeds, rerun it, and change one input at a time. Use only synthetic or appropriately licensed data. Do not add credentials or private information.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Check input shapes, target alignment, data types, missing values, label order, and whether the expected output assumes a fixed random seed. Fit learned preprocessing only on training data, preferably inside a Pipeline. Do not select parameters by repeatedly looking at the final test set.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Anomaly Detection Workflows is part of Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection. Define the task, inspect the inputs, choose a simple reference approach, and test the result on representative examples before drawing conclusions. Use the listed syllabus topics as a checklist, then complete the Try it yourself task. The goal is not to maximize a score at any cost; it is to build a reproducible, fit-for-purpose workflow whose evidence and limits are clear.

content.task: Try it yourself: use a small synthetic or built-in dataset to practice anomaly detection workflows. State the inputs, predicted outcome, assumptions, and one limitation; compare the result with a baseline or a manually traceable expectation where appropriate. A linked practical exercise asks you to produce a reproducible artifact and evidence.
task_acceptance_criteria: Accurately address the lesson topic and its listed syllabus subtopics.
Record the predicted and observed result or a clear manual trace.
State an assumption, failure mode, or limitation and how it was checked.
hints: Write down inputs, expected output, and assumptions before running code.
Keep data splitting, fitting, transformation, and evaluation steps explicit; use reproducible settings when randomness is involved.
Change one condition at a time and document whether the result supports the original hypothesis.
troubleshooting: Run in the project virtual environment and inspect `python -c "import sklearn; print(sklearn.__version__)"`.
If output differs, check package versions, fixed seeds, data order, and input shapes before changing the model.
If the code references a newer API, compare the installed-version API reference and use the supported equivalent rather than guessing.
Examples use toy or built-in data; they do not establish production accuracy or business impact.
